newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia union said growing despite chief's trial.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia union said growing despite chief's trial.

text.p: An international trade union delegation said on Thursday that Indonesia's only independent labour union was growing despite the prosecution of its leader, Mucthar Pakpahan, on subversion charges.

Willy Peirens, president of the Brussels-based World Confederation of Labour (WCL), told a news conference at the end of a two-day visit that the unrecognised Indonesian Labour Welfare Union (SBSI) was getting stronger.

"Despite the very difficult situation the SBSI is working under and despite the pressure of the government, there is a steady growth of the organisation," said Peirens, whose group represents more than 23 million workers in 113 countries.
"The SBSI is becoming bigger and stronger," he added.
Indonesia only recognises the sanctioned All Indonesia Workers Union (SPSI).
SBSI Deputy Chairman Tohap Simanungkalit said the union's listed membership was 150,000 in January this year, but with current growth rates was probably now more than 160,000.
Its membership peaked in 1993 with 500,000 members before official persecution of the union in the wake of the April 1994 Medan racial riots.
The riots followed days of labour unrest and resulted in one death. Union membership fell to only 8,000.

After a series of controversial trials, Pakpahan, who was not in Medan at the time, was sentenced to four years prison in 1994 for inciting the riots. But he was freed and acquitted by the Supreme Court the following year.
However, after riots in Jakarta last July, Pakpahan was one of a number of activists arrested and charged with subversion, which carries the death penalty in Indonesia.

Pakpahan's trial, which is being closely watched by Western diplomats and international labour groups, began last December and has made no reference to the riots. Instead, it has focused on Pakpahan's book, speeches and union activities.
"There is no independent legal system in Indonesia. If you look at the trial and its processes, you can't say it is a fair trial," WCL Vice-President Anton Westerlaken told reporters.

The trial has been suspended until further notice after Pakpahan was admitted to hospital two weeks ago suffering from vertigo, a long-standing ailment. However, subsequent tests have found a tumour in his right lung and further tests are expected in the next few days.

Union sources said John Shattuck, U.S. assistant secretary of state for democracy, human rights and labour, visited Pakpahan on Tuesday and offered medical facilities in the United States. The WCL has also offered to pay for treatment in Europe.

However, the Supreme Court, in a highly controversial decision, re-imposed the original four-year sentence in the Medan case on Pakpahan. His lawyer noted that no one has ever escaped conviction under Indonesia's subversion law.
